newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Thai 1997 car sales seen sliding on economy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thai 1997 car sales seen sliding on economy.

text.p: Thai car sales are expected to fall sharply this year, hit by a severe economic downturn and the government's moves to curb consumer spending, analysts and industry sources said on Thursday.
The sharp fall in car sales would prompt most automakers to reduce output and halt some production for inventory adjustment, they said.

"Most of the automakers which primarily assembled cars for the local market will be affected by the country's recent economic crisis," Tim Dunne, researcher at Bangkok-based Automotive Resources Asia, told Reuters.
"So we could anticipate that automakers would cut their production out of Thailand," he said.
The Thai economy has been in the doldrums as a result of the collapse of an inflated real estate sector, sluggish exports and over-borrowing of short-term foreign debts.

Sales of commercial vehicles and passenger cars this year are now expected to fall to 460,000 units from earlier forecasts of 600,000 and about 580,000 in 1996, according to the Thai Automotive Industry Association.

"The current economic conditions are unfavourable for people to buy new cars. The demand in the second half will not pick up as we earlier expected," said Surapong Paisitpatnapong, spokesman for the association.
Thailand's car market has been growing exponentially at an average rate of about 20 percent a year over the past five to six years, Dunne said.
Many major Japanese car assemblers on Thursday announced a drastic cut in their output in Thailand as a result of the country's sluggish economy and declining sales.
Nissan Motor Co Ltd, which has two factories in Thailand, said it would reduce its output by stopping operations for all of August at a plant which produces pickup trucks.
Nissan's sales in Thailand from January-June were 31,240, down 37.7 percent year-on-year.
Japanese truck maker Hino Motors Ltd was considering suspending production in Thailand from mid-August until the end of September.
It also lowered its sales target in Thailand to 5,500 vehicles from 13,000 for the year ending March 1998 due to the weak economy.

"The suspension of finance companies and three percentage point (increase) in value added tax also compounded the negative impact on the car market," said an auto analyst at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett Asia.
The government this week launched a series of economic measures including the closure of 42 troubled finance firms and the increase in the VAT rate to 10 percent from 7.0 percent.
The move was viewed as an attempt to comply with International Monetary Fund conditions in exchange for IMF financial support, analysts said.

Dunne said the current slowdown in the car industry would not weaken Thailand's position as the car manufacturing base in Asia because the country's competitiveness in the industry remained high compared with other nations in the region.
